newsitem.title: USA: U.S. FDA panel votes down ILEXZ AIDS drug.
newsitem.headline: U.S. FDA panel votes down ILEXZ AIDS drug.

text.p: A U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) advisory panel Monday unanimously voted against approval of ILEX Oncology Inc's mitoguazone dihydrocholoride (Zyrkamine) for AIDS-related non-Hodgkins lymphoma (AR-NHL).

The panel cited doubts about how many patients responded to the therapy and how long the response lasted. AR-NHL is the second most common AIDS-related cancer affecting 10,000 to 20,000 patients, six percent of whom will die of the condition.
ILEX was seeking accelerated approval, which would allow it to market the drug based on early safety and efficacy data.
Sanofi S.A. has licensed worldwide marketing rights from ILEX for the drug.
In its review, FDA questioned the company's data and noted that it had been asked to use a control in the study, but that ILEX declined to do so.
ILEX said that investigators had refused to compare the drug to other regimens, but the company has since submitted plans to do such a trial.

Agency medical reviewer Albert Lin said that the FDA believed that only five patients, not 13 as claimed by ILEX, had responded to therapy. He also said that seven of 37 patient deaths were "possibly" or "probably" related to Zyrkamine.
He called the efficacy of the drug "uncertain" and added that "the risk associated with use of treatment is not negligible."

ILEX applied for FDA approval in October 1996 for Zyrkamine, also known as MGBG. It is the first of a new class of cancer compounds that inhibits a substance key to tumor growth and is intended for use in patients who have failed previous regimens. Patients with AR-NHL are usually treated with combinations of chemotherapy. About 50 percent of tumors respond to these regimens but there is a significant relapse rate and median survival is 35 weeks. There is no standard second line therapy but physicians do have alternatives.

ILEX submitted data from two phase II trials. Patients received two infusions of Zyrkamine in the first week, and then once every two weeks after that, up to either disease progression or 16 weeks after the first response. Six patients (6.7 percent) had a complete remission, seven (7.8 percent) had a greater than 50 percent decrease in tumor size, and 16 patients had no further tumor growth.
The average time to worsening of disease was 40 days, and the median survival was 84 days.

Robert De Lap, director of the division of oncologic products at FDA, noted that it was difficult to evaluate a drug based on such a small number of patients studied -- 90 -- and with so few people actually responding to the therapy.
De Lap said "it's very troublesome to me that more people are sitting around this table than there are responders," but added that he did not blame ILEX for the paucity of data.

Despite what it called "disappointing" survival rates and unimpressive response rate, a group of seven AIDS activist organizations, including AIDS Project Los Angeles, Gay Mens Health Crisis, Project Inform, and the Treatment Action Group, said it supports approval of Zyrkamine.
The consensus was that median survival for responders and those with stable disease, and an "excellent safety profile," warranted approval.
